{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Chronic gastritis", "confidence": 0.85}, {"diagnosis": "Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Peptic ulcer disease", "confidence": 0.72}, {"diagnosis": "Functional dyspepsia", "confidence": 0.65}, {"diagnosis": "Gallstone disease (biliary colic or chronic cholecystitis)", "confidence": 0.6}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.602, "reasoning": "Upper abdominal pain lasting two months suggests a chronic, non-acute process. Common structural and functional gastrointestinal etiologies dominate the differential. Chronic gastritis is highly plausible given its prevalence, association with H. pylori or NSAID use, and insidious onset. GERD often presents with epigastric or retrosternal discomfort and can persist for months without classic heartburn. Peptic ulcer disease remains likely—especially if pain is meal-related or nocturnal—though many ulcers are now asymptomatic or subtle due to widespread PPI use. Functional dyspepsia is a diagnosis of exclusion but common in otherwise healthy adults with persistent epigastric pain and no alarm features; its inclusion reflects the absence of red flags in the limited data. Gallstone disease is included because biliary pain can localize to the epigastrium (not just right upper quadrant), particularly in older adults or those with atypical presentations; however, its lower confidence reflects the lack of associated symptoms (e.g., fatty food intolerance, jaundice, fever) or demographic clues. Less likely diagnoses (e.g., pancreatic cancer, gastric malignancy, autoimmune hepatitis) are excluded from the top 5 due to low pretest probability without alarm features (weight loss, anemia, jaundice, age >55 with new-onset symptoms, or abnormal labs). Further history, physical exam, and testing (e.g., H. pylori testing, endoscopy, LFTs, RUQ ultrasound) are essential to refine this list."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Helicobacter pylori infection", "confidence": 0.95}, {"diagnosis": "NSAID-induced duodenal ulcers", "confidence": 0.88}, {"diagnosis": "Zollinger-Ellison syndrome", "confidence": 0.72}, {"diagnosis": "Crohn's disease (duodenal involvement)", "confidence": 0.45}, {"diagnosis": "Idiopathic duodenal ulcer disease", "confidence": 0.38}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.32, "reasoning": "Multiple duodenal ulcers strongly suggest an underlying ulcerogenic driver. H. pylori is the most common cause of duodenal ulcers globally, with high prevalence in chronic cases; confidence is highest given typical presentation and endoscopic appearance. NSAID use is the second most common cause—highly plausible even without explicit patient history, as it is frequently underreported or subclinical. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) is less common but must be considered in refractory or multiple duodenal ulcers, especially with associated features like hypergastrinemia or diarrhea (not yet assessed); confidence reflects its rarity but clinical significance. Crohn’s disease can involve the duodenum and cause ulceration, but isolated duodenal ulcers without other GI symptoms (e.g., diarrhea, perianal disease) or systemic features make it less likely. Idiopathic duodenal ulcers are a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out H. pylori, NSAIDs, and gastrinoma; low confidence reflects its rarity and requirement for thorough negative workup."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Helicobacter pylori infection", "confidence": 0.92}, {"diagnosis": "NSAID-induced duodenal ulcers", "confidence": 0.85}, {"diagnosis": "Zollinger-Ellison syndrome", "confidence": 0.72}, {"diagnosis": "Crohn disease (upper GI involvement)", "confidence": 0.48}, {"diagnosis": "Idiopathic duodenal ulcer disease", "confidence": 0.35}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 0.912, "reasoning": "Multiple duodenal ulcers are highly specific for H. pylori infection (present in >90% of cases) or NSAID use; given the absence of confirmed negative H. pylori testing *under appropriate test-withdrawal conditions*, H. pylori remains the most likely etiology (confidence 0.92). NSAID-induced ulcers are also highly plausible (0.85), especially if recent exposure occurred but was not disclosed or recalled. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is less common but must be considered in refractory or multiple duodenal ulcers—particularly with persistent symptoms despite standard therapy—hence moderate confidence (0.72). Crohn disease can cause aphthous or linear ulcers in the duodenum, but typically presents with additional features (e.g., diarrhea, weight loss, perianal disease, ileocolonic involvement); absence of such clues lowers confidence to 0.48. Idiopathic duodenal ulcers are rare (<5% of cases after excluding H. pylori and NSAIDs) and diagnosis of exclusion; without definitive exclusion of the two major causes, confidence remains low (0.35)."}
